title: Fair Allocation Over Time, with Applications to Content Moderation

problem.claim: The paper studies the short-term planning problem of allocating human content reviewers across harmful content categories.

contributions.claim: The paper applies competitive equilibrium and leximin allocation rules to fair allocation of content reviewers.

The paper develops a workload-constrained allocation formulation inspired by the Eisenberg-Gale program that satisfies forecasted workloads and fairly allocates remaining reviewer hours across content categories.
The paper extends fair allocation approaches to time-dependent allocation and investigates smooth allocations that limit staffing changes over time.

stated_novelty.claim: The paper explicitly introduces novel practical aspects to the traditional Fisher market setup, including forecasted workloads and time-dependent allocation extensions.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that their Eisenberg-Gale-inspired formulation satisfies forecasted workload constraints and fairly allocates remaining working hours.
The authors report that many properties of the single-time-period fair allocation approaches extend to the time-dependent setting, with modifications.
The authors report demonstrating the performance of their approaches using real-world data obtained from Meta.

narrative_sequence.summary: Content moderation is important and requires efficient planning because of the volume of online content.
The paper studies short-term allocation of human reviewers across harmful content categories using fair division tools.
The approach incorporates forecasted category workloads and fairly allocates reviewer-hour oversupply, providing a guardrail when actual workload differs from forecasts.
The paper extends fair allocation to reviewer scheduling across days and considers smooth allocations to minimize staffing switches.
The proposed approaches are demonstrated using real-world data from Meta.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the formal optimization objectives, constraints, or allocation rules in detail.
The abstract does not report quantitative evaluation results, baselines, dataset size, or experimental outcomes.
